Rewriting the future of women's health November 1, 2026 | Sunday | Analysis | By Ayesha Siddiqui Women's health is emerging as a critical frontier for healthcare innovation across Asia-Pacific. From non-invasive diagnostics for endometriosis and advances in cancer care to personalised menopause management and AI-driven healthcare, new technologies are beginning to address longstanding gaps in diagnosis, treatment and patient support. Yet, despite this progress, underinvestment in research, limited clinical evidence and unequal access continue to constrain the impact of these advances. As the region's life-sciences ecosystem expands, the challenge is no longer just to develop innovative solutions, but to translate scientific breakthroughs into accessible, evidence-based care that improves health outcomes for women across their lives. image credit- shutterstock Women's health remains one of healthcare's most significant unmet needs, despite advances in diagnostics, treatments and digital technologies. Conditions that are specific to women, disproportionately affect them or manifest differently by sex continue to impose a substantial burden on individuals, healthcare systems and economies. The McKinsey Health Institute (MHI) has assessed 64 conditions that collectively account for more than 85 per cent of the global disease burden among women. The opportunity to address this gap is considerable. The World Economic Forum (WEF) and MHI examined nine conditions, including breast and cervical cancer, menopausal symptoms, migraine, endometriosis and maternal health conditions, that together account for roughly one-third of the women's health gap. Addressing these conditions could deliver nearly 27 million additional disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) annually and generate $400 billion in annual economic gains by 2040. Across Asia-Pacific, innovation is beginning to reshape how women's health conditions are detected, managed and treated. Non-invasive diagnostics are seeking to reduce delays in identifying endometriosis; molecular tests are opening new possibilities in cancer detection; and digital platforms are expanding access to menopause guidance, fertility services and personalised health information. Artificial intelligence (AI) is also creating opportunities to support screening, clinical decision-making and patient engagement. Yet scientific progress alone cannot close the women's health gap. Many promising technologies still require stronger clinical evidence, while funding constraints, uneven healthcare infrastructure, limited awareness and affordability continue to restrict access. The challenge is particularly significant in a region as diverse as Asia-Pacific, where research capabilities, regulatory environments and access to healthcare vary widely. In this story we examine innovations across four areas—endometriosis, next-generation women's cancer care, menopause management and AI-driven personalised healthcare—and assesses how far they have advanced diagnosis, treatment and patient outcomes. It also explores the investment, research and health-system changes needed to ensure that scientific advances translate into accessible, effective care for women across the region. Endometriosis: Shortening the Diagnostic Journey Women's health innovation across Asia-Pacific is increasingly focused on improving the diagnosis and treatment of conditions that have historically been under-recognised. Endometriosis remains a significant challenge, affecting an estimated 190 million women worldwide, or around 10 per cent of women of reproductive age, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Diagnosis can be delayed by four to 12 years, prolonging pain, disrupting daily life and delaying appropriate treatment. In Australia, the average diagnostic delay is estimated at six to eight years. The burden is also reflected in healthcare spending and hospital admissions. Health-system expenditure attributable to endometriosis reached an estimated A$293 million in 2022–23, more than double the 2013–14 figure. In 2024–25, Australia recorded 24,700 endometriosis hospitalisations, with the hospitalisation rate increasing by 23 per cent over the preceding decade. “One of the main challenges is diagnostic uncertainty. Pelvic pain is common and can have several causes, while endometriosis symptoms often overlap with those of other conditions. Symptom severity also does not necessarily reflect the extent of the disease. Although ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help identify endometriosis, they do not always establish the cause of a patient's symptoms. Surgery can provide further diagnostic information but is invasive. The WHO has therefore identified non-invasive diagnosis as an important area for improvement,” said David Morris, CEO, Proteomics International . The Australian precision diagnostics company is seeking to address this gap through PromarkerEndo, a non-invasive blood test designed to assess the likelihood of endometriosis. The test uses mass spectrometry to measure protein biomarkers and combines the results with clinical factors through a fixed algorithm to classify patients as having a low, moderate or high risk of the disease. “The model was developed using samples from The Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne and independently validated using more than 400 samples from the University of Oxford,” said Morris. The validation study reported 90 per cent sensitivity for stage IV disease, 84 per cent for stages III–IV, 80 per cent for stages II–IV and 68 per cent across all stages, with 71 per cent specificity across the stage groupings. The results indicate that performance varies with disease stage, underlining the importance of further clinical evaluation and appropriate use within diagnostic pathways. Other Australian companies are exploring complementary approaches. ELEN MedTech is developing a handheld diagnostic platform aimed at detecting superficial peritoneal endometriosis, a form of the disease that can be difficult to identify. Meanwhile, researchers are investigating the genetic factors that may contribute to disease susceptibility and influence risk across different populations. In September 2026, researchers in India reported work under the Endometriosis Clinical and Genetic Research in India (ECGRI) initiative, led by Dr Rahul K. Gajbhiye, Scientist E and Head of the Clinical Research Laboratory at ICMR–NIRWoH. The multicentre study involved 18 centres and included women with surgically confirmed endometriosis and control participants from diverse regional and socioeconomic backgrounds. The research aims to establish baseline evidence on genetic risk factors among Indian women and support future investigations into disease mechanisms, early diagnosis and personalised treatment. While diagnostic research seeks to identify the condition sooner, drug developers are working to expand treatment options, particularly for women who need alternatives to existing hormonal therapies. In March 2026, China's Hope Medicine announced that the first patient had been dosed in a Phase III clinical trial of HMI-115, an investigational monoclonal antibody being developed for endometriosis-associated pain. The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial has a 24-week treatment period and is designed to assess the safety and efficacy of HMI-115 in treating moderate-to-severe pain. Its development as a non-hormonal treatment could offer another approach to managing the condition if clinical trials establish an acceptable safety profile and meaningful clinical benefit. Innovation must also extend beyond products to the healthcare systems through which patients receive care. Australia has expanded its network of endometriosis and pelvic pain clinics from 22 to 33, aiming to improve access to earlier diagnosis, treatment and specialist referrals. Its broader women's health package also includes subsidised contraceptives and menopausal hormone therapies, as well as Medicare-funded menopause health assessments. By February 2026, more than 660,000 women had accessed over two million lower-cost prescriptions for contraception, menopause hormone therapy and endometriosis treatment. New Zealand has also updated its clinical guidelines. Introduced in August 2026, the guidelines support clinicians in making a diagnosis based on symptoms, family history and examination without requiring laparoscopic surgery in every case. General practitioners can begin appropriate treatment and refer patients for specialist care when necessary. The government is also developing training and resources to help primary care professionals recognise the condition. Together, these developments illustrate the three requirements for progress in endometriosis care: more timely diagnosis, better treatment choices and clinical pathways that help women access appropriate care without prolonged delays. The Next Generation of Women's Cancer Care Advances in women's cancer care, particularly in breast and ovarian cancer, have improved diagnosis and treatment, allowing many patients to live longer after diagnosis. The next challenge is to extend those gains beyond survival, addressing treatment-related complications and helping survivors maintain their health and quality of life. “Many survivors carry lasting side effects from the treatments that saved their lives. Heart damage from certain chemotherapies is one example, and it can limit a person's ability to work, exercise or care for their family. As more women survive their cancer, the field is increasingly focused not just on treating the cancer, but on helping patients stay healthy enough to enjoy full, active lives,” said Daniel Tillet, CEO, Racura Oncology . He added, “This shift is driving real innovation. Researchers are developing new therapies that are both more effective at controlling cancer and gentler on the body, giving women the best chance of completing their treatment and returning to their families, careers and communities in good health.” Australian biotechnology company Racura Oncology is exploring this approach through RC220, an investigational anticancer drug. Alongside its work on cancer treatment, the company is investigating whether RC220 could help protect patients against chemotherapy-induced heart damage through its Cardioprotection and Anticancer Synergy (CPACS) trial. The research reflects a wider effort to develop treatments that address cancer while reducing the risk of serious side effects. The clinical benefits of RC220 will need to be established through further research. Diagnostics represent another important frontier, particularly in distinguishing benign from malignant conditions and helping clinicians make more informed treatment decisions. Singapore-based INEX Innovate, a women's health molecular diagnostics company spun out of the National University of Singapore, is developing tests for several women's cancers. Its OvaCis test is designed for use during ovarian cyst surgery. It measures haptoglobin levels in cyst fluid to help distinguish benign from malignant ovarian cysts, with results available in approximately five minutes. The test has received regulatory approval from Singapore's Health Sciences Authority. INEX Innovate is also developing epiHERA for endometrial cancer, epiDX, a blood-based liquid biopsy test using epigenetic markers for breast cancer detection and stratification, and XENA for ovarian cancer evaluation. These technologies target different stages of the diagnostic pathway, although their clinical applications and evidence bases vary. In Australia, Cleo Diagnostics is developing AdnexaSure, a blood test that uses the CXCL10 biomarker to help distinguish benign from malignant ovarian growths. If adequately validated, the approach could provide additional information when evaluating ovarian masses and help guide decisions on further investigation. The impact of these technologies will depend on more than their technical performance. Clinical validation, appropriate regulatory pathways, affordability and integration into established care are essential if new tests are to improve patient management and outcomes. Prevention remains equally important. Singapore plans to introduce subsidies for genetic testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer from December 2026. In India, a nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign launched in February 2026, offering free, voluntary single-dose vaccination to around 1.15 crore girls aged 14. By September, more than 80 lakh doses had reportedly been administered. These initiatives highlight the breadth of the opportunity in women's cancer care, spanning prevention, early detection, treatment and survivorship. The next phase will depend on ensuring that advances across this pathway are supported by robust evidence and accessible healthcare services. Menopause: From Symptom Management to Midlife Health Menopause and midlife health are receiving greater attention across Asia-Pacific, where limited region-specific research, cultural stigma and gaps in clinical care have left many women without adequate support. The focus is expanding beyond symptom management to include workplace wellbeing, pelvic health and the longer-term effects of hormonal changes on women's health. A 2025 white paper, Menopause and the Bottom Line: A Critical Leadership Challenge for APAC Leaders , examined the experiences of 1,741 working women across Singapore, Vietnam, Australia, Japan and Indonesia. Published by the Asia Centre for Reproductive Longevity and Equality at the National University of Singapore and HeyVenus Integrated Healthscience, the study sought to address gaps in evidence on how women across the region experience menopause. Nearly half of the women surveyed reported significant disruptions to work performance and daily activities, including fatigue, forgetfulness and difficulty maintaining focus. The findings highlight how menopausal symptoms can affect not only quality of life but also workplace participation and productivity. The need for culturally relevant information and support is creating opportunities for digital health solutions. Singapore-based HeyVenus provides digital symptom tracking and personalised menopause guidance, while Sol offers menopause information and support tailored to Asian women. Such platforms can help women understand symptoms and prepare for clinical consultations, although digital guidance needs to complement, rather than replace, evidence-based medical care. Governments and healthcare institutions are also working to improve the consistency of treatment. In Australia, the government opened the tender process in October 2025 to develop the country's first national clinical guidelines for perimenopause and menopause. The initiative aims to improve diagnosis and treatment and address gaps in healthcare professionals' knowledge of menopause management and hormone therapy. In Singapore, SingHealth has introduced menopause management guidelines to address inconsistent care and the under-recognition of symptoms. Research is also examining the wider metabolic changes associated with midlife. In August 2026, Haleon and Singapore's Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) launched a clinical study investigating metabolic health in midlife Asian women. The work could contribute to a better understanding of health changes during this stage of life and inform future approaches to prevention and care. The challenge is to translate growing awareness into accessible clinical services. Digital tools, clinical guidelines and emerging research can contribute to better menopause care, but their benefits will depend on the availability of trained healthcare professionals, reliable information and appropriate treatment options. AI and Personalised Care: New Possibilities, New Questions Artificial intelligence is creating opportunities to personalise women's healthcare across Asia-Pacific, from cervical cancer prevention and fertility treatment to menstrual health and access to gynaecological care. However, the significance of these applications depends on the clinical problem they address, the evidence supporting their use and their ability to reach patients who need them. In China, a randomised controlled trial involving 2,671 parents in Shanghai and Anhui Province found that an AI chatbot providing personalised information on HPV vaccination increased vaccine uptake and engagement with healthcare professionals. The findings suggest that AI-enabled communication could help address information gaps and support preventive healthcare, although its effectiveness will depend on the populations served and how such tools are integrated into vaccination programmes. In Australia, Ovum AI's Ovum Brain is designed to track women's health information across symptoms, reproductive health, medication, appointments, lifestyle, diet and fitness. By helping users identify patterns over time, the platform aims to support more informed conversations about their health. In India, Pinky Promise uses an AI-assisted, chat-first model to connect women with registered doctors for Rs 99 consultations and reports having reached more than 400,000 women. The model illustrates how digital platforms may lower barriers to initial consultations, although the quality of care also depends on clinical oversight, appropriate referrals and access to follow-up services. AI is also being applied in fertility care. South Korea's Kai Health develops AI-assisted embryo assessment technology for in vitro fertilisation (IVF). Thailand's Inspire IVF uses AI-integrated telemedicine to connect patients with fertility specialists and support treatment planning. These applications demonstrate the range of ways in which AI could support women's healthcare, but they should not be treated as equivalent in their clinical maturity. Consumer-facing symptom tracking, digital consultations, communication tools and AI-assisted clinical assessment serve different purposes and require different levels of validation. For AI to deliver meaningful improvements, systems must be evaluated for accuracy, safety and clinical usefulness. Data quality, representation of diverse populations, privacy safeguards and appropriate human oversight will be critical. Without these safeguards, digital innovation could reproduce existing disparities rather than reduce them. The wider opportunity lies in combining technology with accessible healthcare services, enabling women to move from information and initial assessment to appropriate diagnosis, treatment and long-term support. Has Innovation Delivered Sufficient Progress? The developments across endometriosis, cancer care, menopause and AI-enabled healthcare demonstrate that women's health innovation is expanding across Asia-Pacific. New diagnostic approaches, investigational therapies and digital platforms are addressing needs that have historically received insufficient attention. However, the number of technologies in development is not, by itself, a measure of progress. The more important question is whether these innovations are changing clinical practice and improving outcomes. Can they shorten diagnostic delays, enable more effective treatment decisions, reduce complications and reach women who have limited access to specialist care? Answering these questions requires robust clinical validation, evidence of real-world effectiveness and healthcare systems capable of integrating new solutions into routine practice. Across the region, these requirements remain unevenly met. Funding constraints, gaps in professional training, limited awareness and disparities in healthcare access continue to restrict the benefits of innovation. “Despite significant progress, major gaps remain in maternal health, reproductive care, fertility management, and access to quality diagnostics. Preventable maternal deaths and disparities in healthcare access continue to affect many communities across the APAC region,” said SoonPil Kyon, VP & GM, Commercial GGM (Global Growth Market), Revvity . Bridging these gaps requires more than developing new technologies. Education, healthcare professional training, public awareness and long-term partnerships are also essential to translating innovation into better health outcomes. “The greatest impact comes when innovation is combined with education, healthcare professional training, public awareness, and long-term partnerships. A strong example is the Philippines, which recently marked 30 years of newborn screening. What began in a small number of hospitals has grown into a national public health programme that now screens more than 97 per cent of newborns for 29 disorders,” said Kyon. The importance of this approach is also evident in the need to reduce delays between the onset of symptoms and appropriate care. As Morris observed, “The broader goal, however, is not simply to introduce another test – innovation does not happen in a silo. Women's health innovation needs to improve the patient journey. That means moving towards earlier recognition, greater diagnostic clarity, appropriately targeted referrals and treatment, and fewer years spent seeking answers.” This patient-centred approach offers a useful measure of progress. Innovation must be judged not only by the technologies developed, but also by whether they improve the experience of care and deliver measurable benefits across diverse populations. What Will Define the Next Phase? The next phase of women's health innovation will depend on sustained investment, stronger research and better translation of discoveries into clinical practice. Research and development in this field has long been underfunded. According to the World Economic Forum, companies focused exclusively on women's health attracted less than 1 per cent of private healthcare investment between 2020 and 2025. The WEF's Women's Health Innovation Radar: Revealing Gaps and Opportunities Across the Science-to-Patient Journey , developed in collaboration with the Global Alliance for Women's Health, the Kearney Health Institute, the Gates Foundation and Wellcome Leap, identifies three major gaps in the innovation pipeline. The allocation gap: Only around 20 per cent of research funding across the 10 conditions analysed is women-focused, with more than half of this funding concentrated in ovarian cancer and menopause. The evidence gap: Women-focused research accounts for only 16 per cent of scientific publications and fewer than 3 per cent of clinical trials across the conditions studied. The translation gap: Research does not consistently translate into scalable solutions, with product development concentrated in a limited number of conditions. Together, these gaps reveal a mismatch between disease burden and innovation priorities. Conditions such as ischaemic heart disease, migraine and mental health disorders, which contribute substantially to the burden of disease among women, continue to receive comparatively limited targeted funding, research and product development. Endometriosis, menopause and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) also remain underfunded relative to their impact. In Asia-Pacific, access to finance presents an additional challenge, particularly for femtech startups seeking to develop and scale their solutions. The United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UN ESCAP), in its December 2025 report Femtech in South-East Asia: Unlocking Innovation for Women's Health , identified funding and investment as major barriers for businesses in the sector. Between 2019 and 2024, femtech startups in Australia raised 140.7 million, while businesses across Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Viet Nam collectively raised $32.9 million. Of the latter amount, 96 per cent went to Singapore-headquartered companies, highlighting the concentration of investment within the region. The figures point to the need for a broader funding ecosystem that enables businesses across different markets to develop, validate and scale solutions. Capital alone, however, will not close the gap. Investment needs to support the full journey from identifying unmet clinical needs and conducting research to validating products, securing regulatory approvals and integrating solutions into healthcare systems. Stronger collaboration between researchers, hospitals, industry and investors can help ensure that products are developed around clearly defined clinical requirements rather than technology availability alone. The WEF's innovation analysis also highlights the need to direct funding towards conditions with a high disease burden, strengthen the evidence base focused on women's health and expand product development beyond established areas. For Asia-Pacific, this means generating more region-specific evidence, improving the availability and governance of health data, and supporting clinical research that reflects the region's diverse populations. UN ESCAP recommends increasing funding for women's health research, raising awareness, addressing social taboos and supporting sector-specific incubators, accelerators and networks. Grants and other forms of financial support will be important in helping femtech businesses develop and scale their solutions. Healthcare systems must also ensure that promising innovations can be adopted beyond well-resourced urban centres. “Looking ahead, the next phase of progress in women's health will depend not only on scientific breakthroughs but also on ensuring broader access to those innovations. Expanding screening programmes, strengthening healthcare systems, generating more APAC-specific evidence, and investing in education and clinical capabilities will be essential to improving outcomes for women and families across the region,” said Kyon. The economic case for action is substantial. The WEF and MHI report Closing the Women's Health Gap: A $1 Trillion Opportunity to Improve Lives and Economies found that women spend 25 per cent more of their lives in poor health than men. Closing the broader women's health gap could deliver 75 million additional disability-adjusted life years annually and unlock $1 trillion in global GDP each year by 2040. For Asia-Pacific, the opportunity is not simply to develop more products or adopt new technologies. It is to build a healthcare ecosystem in which women's health needs shape research priorities, clinical evidence guides decisions and innovation reaches the patients it is intended to serve. The next frontier will be defined by how effectively the region turns scientific progress into equitable, measurable and lasting improvements in women's lives. Women's health remains one of healthcare's most significant unmet needs, despite advances in diagnostics, treatments and digital technologies. Conditions that are specific to women, disproportionately affect them or manifest differently by sex continue to impose a substantial burden on individuals, healthcare systems and economies. The McKinsey Health Institute (MHI) has assessed 64 conditions that collectively account for more than 85 per cent of the global disease burden among women.
The opportunity to address this gap is considerable. The World Economic Forum (WEF) and MHI examined nine conditions, including breast and cervical cancer, menopausal symptoms, migraine, endometriosis and maternal health conditions, that together account for roughly one-third of the women's health gap. Addressing these conditions could deliver nearly 27 million additional disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) annually and generate $400 billion in annual economic gains by 2040.
Across Asia-Pacific, innovation is beginning to reshape how women's health conditions are detected, managed and treated. Non-invasive diagnostics are seeking to reduce delays in identifying endometriosis; molecular tests are opening new possibilities in cancer detection; and digital platforms are expanding access to menopause guidance, fertility services and personalised health information. Artificial intelligence (AI) is also creating opportunities to support screening, clinical decision-making and patient engagement.
Yet scientific progress alone cannot close the women's health gap. Many promising technologies still require stronger clinical evidence, while funding constraints, uneven healthcare infrastructure, limited awareness and affordability continue to restrict access. The challenge is particularly significant in a region as diverse as Asia-Pacific, where research capabilities, regulatory environments and access to healthcare vary widely.
In this story we examine innovations across four areas—endometriosis, next-generation women's cancer care, menopause management and AI-driven personalised healthcare—and assesses how far they have advanced diagnosis, treatment and patient outcomes. It also explores the investment, research and health-system changes needed to ensure that scientific advances translate into accessible, effective care for women across the region.
Endometriosis: Shortening the Diagnostic Journey
Women's health innovation across Asia-Pacific is increasingly focused on improving the diagnosis and treatment of conditions that have historically been under-recognised. Endometriosis remains a significant challenge, affecting an estimated 190 million women worldwide, or around 10 per cent of women of reproductive age, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Diagnosis can be delayed by four to 12 years, prolonging pain, disrupting daily life and delaying appropriate treatment.
In Australia, the average diagnostic delay is estimated at six to eight years. The burden is also reflected in healthcare spending and hospital admissions. Health-system expenditure attributable to endometriosis reached an estimated A$293 million in 2022–23, more than double the 2013–14 figure. In 2024–25, Australia recorded 24,700 endometriosis hospitalisations, with the hospitalisation rate increasing by 23 per cent over the preceding decade.
“One of the main challenges is diagnostic uncertainty. Pelvic pain is common and can have several causes, while endometriosis symptoms often overlap with those of other conditions. Symptom severity also does not necessarily reflect the extent of the disease. Although ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help identify endometriosis, they do not always establish the cause of a patient's symptoms. Surgery can provide further diagnostic information but is invasive. The WHO has therefore identified non-invasive diagnosis as an important area for improvement,” said David Morris, CEO, Proteomics International .
David Morris, CEO, Proteomics International
The Australian precision diagnostics company is seeking to address this gap through PromarkerEndo, a non-invasive blood test designed to assess the likelihood of endometriosis. The test uses mass spectrometry to measure protein biomarkers and combines the results with clinical factors through a fixed algorithm to classify patients as having a low, moderate or high risk of the disease.
“The model was developed using samples from The Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne and independently validated using more than 400 samples from the University of Oxford,” said Morris.
The validation study reported 90 per cent sensitivity for stage IV disease, 84 per cent for stages III–IV, 80 per cent for stages II–IV and 68 per cent across all stages, with 71 per cent specificity across the stage groupings. The results indicate that performance varies with disease stage, underlining the importance of further clinical evaluation and appropriate use within diagnostic pathways.
Other Australian companies are exploring complementary approaches. ELEN MedTech is developing a handheld diagnostic platform aimed at detecting superficial peritoneal endometriosis, a form of the disease that can be difficult to identify. Meanwhile, researchers are investigating the genetic factors that may contribute to disease susceptibility and influence risk across different populations.
In September 2026, researchers in India reported work under the Endometriosis Clinical and Genetic Research in India (ECGRI) initiative, led by Dr Rahul K. Gajbhiye, Scientist E and Head of the Clinical Research Laboratory at ICMR–NIRWoH. The multicentre study involved 18 centres and included women with surgically confirmed endometriosis and control participants from diverse regional and socioeconomic backgrounds. The research aims to establish baseline evidence on genetic risk factors among Indian women and support future investigations into disease mechanisms, early diagnosis and personalised treatment.
While diagnostic research seeks to identify the condition sooner, drug developers are working to expand treatment options, particularly for women who need alternatives to existing hormonal therapies.
In March 2026, China's Hope Medicine announced that the first patient had been dosed in a Phase III clinical trial of HMI-115, an investigational monoclonal antibody being developed for endometriosis-associated pain. The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial has a 24-week treatment period and is designed to assess the safety and efficacy of HMI-115 in treating moderate-to-severe pain. Its development as a non-hormonal treatment could offer another approach to managing the condition if clinical trials establish an acceptable safety profile and meaningful clinical benefit.
Innovation must also extend beyond products to the healthcare systems through which patients receive care. Australia has expanded its network of endometriosis and pelvic pain clinics from 22 to 33, aiming to improve access to earlier diagnosis, treatment and specialist referrals. Its broader women's health package also includes subsidised contraceptives and menopausal hormone therapies, as well as Medicare-funded menopause health assessments. By February 2026, more than 660,000 women had accessed over two million lower-cost prescriptions for contraception, menopause hormone therapy and endometriosis treatment.
New Zealand has also updated its clinical guidelines. Introduced in August 2026, the guidelines support clinicians in making a diagnosis based on symptoms, family history and examination without requiring laparoscopic surgery in every case. General practitioners can begin appropriate treatment and refer patients for specialist care when necessary. The government is also developing training and resources to help primary care professionals recognise the condition.
Together, these developments illustrate the three requirements for progress in endometriosis care: more timely diagnosis, better treatment choices and clinical pathways that help women access appropriate care without prolonged delays.
The Next Generation of Women's Cancer Care
Advances in women's cancer care, particularly in breast and ovarian cancer, have improved diagnosis and treatment, allowing many patients to live longer after diagnosis. The next challenge is to extend those gains beyond survival, addressing treatment-related complications and helping survivors maintain their health and quality of life.
“Many survivors carry lasting side effects from the treatments that saved their lives. Heart damage from certain chemotherapies is one example, and it can limit a person's ability to work, exercise or care for their family. As more women survive their cancer, the field is increasingly focused not just on treating the cancer, but on helping patients stay healthy enough to enjoy full, active lives,” said Daniel Tillet, CEO, Racura Oncology .
Daniel Tillet, CEO, Racura Oncology
He added, “This shift is driving real innovation. Researchers are developing new therapies that are both more effective at controlling cancer and gentler on the body, giving women the best chance of completing their treatment and returning to their families, careers and communities in good health.”
Australian biotechnology company Racura Oncology is exploring this approach through RC220, an investigational anticancer drug. Alongside its work on cancer treatment, the company is investigating whether RC220 could help protect patients against chemotherapy-induced heart damage through its Cardioprotection and Anticancer Synergy (CPACS) trial. The research reflects a wider effort to develop treatments that address cancer while reducing the risk of serious side effects. The clinical benefits of RC220 will need to be established through further research.
Diagnostics represent another important frontier, particularly in distinguishing benign from malignant conditions and helping clinicians make more informed treatment decisions.
Singapore-based INEX Innovate, a women's health molecular diagnostics company spun out of the National University of Singapore, is developing tests for several women's cancers. Its OvaCis test is designed for use during ovarian cyst surgery. It measures haptoglobin levels in cyst fluid to help distinguish benign from malignant ovarian cysts, with results available in approximately five minutes. The test has received regulatory approval from Singapore's Health Sciences Authority.
INEX Innovate is also developing epiHERA for endometrial cancer, epiDX, a blood-based liquid biopsy test using epigenetic markers for breast cancer detection and stratification, and XENA for ovarian cancer evaluation. These technologies target different stages of the diagnostic pathway, although their clinical applications and evidence bases vary.
In Australia, Cleo Diagnostics is developing AdnexaSure, a blood test that uses the CXCL10 biomarker to help distinguish benign from malignant ovarian growths. If adequately validated, the approach could provide additional information when evaluating ovarian masses and help guide decisions on further investigation.
The impact of these technologies will depend on more than their technical performance. Clinical validation, appropriate regulatory pathways, affordability and integration into established care are essential if new tests are to improve patient management and outcomes.
Prevention remains equally important. Singapore plans to introduce subsidies for genetic testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer from December 2026. In India, a nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign launched in February 2026, offering free, voluntary single-dose vaccination to around 1.15 crore girls aged 14. By September, more than 80 lakh doses had reportedly been administered.
These initiatives highlight the breadth of the opportunity in women's cancer care, spanning prevention, early detection, treatment and survivorship. The next phase will depend on ensuring that advances across this pathway are supported by robust evidence and accessible healthcare services.
Menopause: From Symptom Management to Midlife Health
Menopause and midlife health are receiving greater attention across Asia-Pacific, where limited region-specific research, cultural stigma and gaps in clinical care have left many women without adequate support. The focus is expanding beyond symptom management to include workplace wellbeing, pelvic health and the longer-term effects of hormonal changes on women's health.
A 2025 white paper, Menopause and the Bottom Line: A Critical Leadership Challenge for APAC Leaders , examined the experiences of 1,741 working women across Singapore, Vietnam, Australia, Japan and Indonesia. Published by the Asia Centre for Reproductive Longevity and Equality at the National University of Singapore and HeyVenus Integrated Healthscience, the study sought to address gaps in evidence on how women across the region experience menopause.

Nearly half of the women surveyed reported significant disruptions to work performance and daily activities, including fatigue, forgetfulness and difficulty maintaining focus. The findings highlight how menopausal symptoms can affect not only quality of life but also workplace participation and productivity.
The need for culturally relevant information and support is creating opportunities for digital health solutions. Singapore-based HeyVenus provides digital symptom tracking and personalised menopause guidance, while Sol offers menopause information and support tailored to Asian women. Such platforms can help women understand symptoms and prepare for clinical consultations, although digital guidance needs to complement, rather than replace, evidence-based medical care.
Governments and healthcare institutions are also working to improve the consistency of treatment. In Australia, the government opened the tender process in October 2025 to develop the country's first national clinical guidelines for perimenopause and menopause. The initiative aims to improve diagnosis and treatment and address gaps in healthcare professionals' knowledge of menopause management and hormone therapy. In Singapore, SingHealth has introduced menopause management guidelines to address inconsistent care and the under-recognition of symptoms.
Research is also examining the wider metabolic changes associated with midlife. In August 2026, Haleon and Singapore's Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) launched a clinical study investigating metabolic health in midlife Asian women. The work could contribute to a better understanding of health changes during this stage of life and inform future approaches to prevention and care.
The challenge is to translate growing awareness into accessible clinical services. Digital tools, clinical guidelines and emerging research can contribute to better menopause care, but their benefits will depend on the availability of trained healthcare professionals, reliable information and appropriate treatment options.
AI and Personalised Care: New Possibilities, New Questions
Artificial intelligence is creating opportunities to personalise women's healthcare across Asia-Pacific, from cervical cancer prevention and fertility treatment to menstrual health and access to gynaecological care. However, the significance of these applications depends on the clinical problem they address, the evidence supporting their use and their ability to reach patients who need them.
In China, a randomised controlled trial involving 2,671 parents in Shanghai and Anhui Province found that an AI chatbot providing personalised information on HPV vaccination increased vaccine uptake and engagement with healthcare professionals. The findings suggest that AI-enabled communication could help address information gaps and support preventive healthcare, although its effectiveness will depend on the populations served and how such tools are integrated into vaccination programmes.
In Australia, Ovum AI's Ovum Brain is designed to track women's health information across symptoms, reproductive health, medication, appointments, lifestyle, diet and fitness. By helping users identify patterns over time, the platform aims to support more informed conversations about their health.
In India, Pinky Promise uses an AI-assisted, chat-first model to connect women with registered doctors for Rs 99 consultations and reports having reached more than 400,000 women. The model illustrates how digital platforms may lower barriers to initial consultations, although the quality of care also depends on clinical oversight, appropriate referrals and access to follow-up services.
AI is also being applied in fertility care. South Korea's Kai Health develops AI-assisted embryo assessment technology for in vitro fertilisation (IVF). Thailand's Inspire IVF uses AI-integrated telemedicine to connect patients with fertility specialists and support treatment planning.
These applications demonstrate the range of ways in which AI could support women's healthcare, but they should not be treated as equivalent in their clinical maturity. Consumer-facing symptom tracking, digital consultations, communication tools and AI-assisted clinical assessment serve different purposes and require different levels of validation.
For AI to deliver meaningful improvements, systems must be evaluated for accuracy, safety and clinical usefulness. Data quality, representation of diverse populations, privacy safeguards and appropriate human oversight will be critical. Without these safeguards, digital innovation could reproduce existing disparities rather than reduce them.
The wider opportunity lies in combining technology with accessible healthcare services, enabling women to move from information and initial assessment to appropriate diagnosis, treatment and long-term support.
Has Innovation Delivered Sufficient Progress?
The developments across endometriosis, cancer care, menopause and AI-enabled healthcare demonstrate that women's health innovation is expanding across Asia-Pacific. New diagnostic approaches, investigational therapies and digital platforms are addressing needs that have historically received insufficient attention. However, the number of technologies in development is not, by itself, a measure of progress.
The more important question is whether these innovations are changing clinical practice and improving outcomes. Can they shorten diagnostic delays, enable more effective treatment decisions, reduce complications and reach women who have limited access to specialist care? Answering these questions requires robust clinical validation, evidence of real-world effectiveness and healthcare systems capable of integrating new solutions into routine practice.
Across the region, these requirements remain unevenly met. Funding constraints, gaps in professional training, limited awareness and disparities in healthcare access continue to restrict the benefits of innovation.
“Despite significant progress, major gaps remain in maternal health, reproductive care, fertility management, and access to quality diagnostics. Preventable maternal deaths and disparities in healthcare access continue to affect many communities across the APAC region,” said SoonPil Kyon, VP & GM, Commercial GGM (Global Growth Market), Revvity .
SoonPil Kyon, VP & GM, Commercial GGM (Global Growth Market), Revvity
Bridging these gaps requires more than developing new technologies. Education, healthcare professional training, public awareness and long-term partnerships are also essential to translating innovation into better health outcomes.
“The greatest impact comes when innovation is combined with education, healthcare professional training, public awareness, and long-term partnerships. A strong example is the Philippines, which recently marked 30 years of newborn screening. What began in a small number of hospitals has grown into a national public health programme that now screens more than 97 per cent of newborns for 29 disorders,” said Kyon.
The importance of this approach is also evident in the need to reduce delays between the onset of symptoms and appropriate care. As Morris observed, “The broader goal, however, is not simply to introduce another test – innovation does not happen in a silo. Women's health innovation needs to improve the patient journey. That means moving towards earlier recognition, greater diagnostic clarity, appropriately targeted referrals and treatment, and fewer years spent seeking answers.”
This patient-centred approach offers a useful measure of progress. Innovation must be judged not only by the technologies developed, but also by whether they improve the experience of care and deliver measurable benefits across diverse populations.
What Will Define the Next Phase?
The next phase of women's health innovation will depend on sustained investment, stronger research and better translation of discoveries into clinical practice. Research and development in this field has long been underfunded. According to the World Economic Forum, companies focused exclusively on women's health attracted less than 1 per cent of private healthcare investment between 2020 and 2025.
The WEF's Women's Health Innovation Radar: Revealing Gaps and Opportunities Across the Science-to-Patient Journey , developed in collaboration with the Global Alliance for Women's Health, the Kearney Health Institute, the Gates Foundation and Wellcome Leap, identifies three major gaps in the innovation pipeline.

Together, these gaps reveal a mismatch between disease burden and innovation priorities. Conditions such as ischaemic heart disease, migraine and mental health disorders, which contribute substantially to the burden of disease among women, continue to receive comparatively limited targeted funding, research and product development. Endometriosis, menopause and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) also remain underfunded relative to their impact.
In Asia-Pacific, access to finance presents an additional challenge, particularly for femtech startups seeking to develop and scale their solutions. The United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UN ESCAP), in its December 2025 report Femtech in South-East Asia: Unlocking Innovation for Women's Health , identified funding and investment as major barriers for businesses in the sector.

Femtech in South-East Asia: Unlocking Innovation for Women's Health
, identified funding and investment as major barriers for businesses in the sector.
Between 2019 and 2024, femtech startups in Australia raised 140.7 million, while businesses across Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Viet Nam collectively raised $32.9 million. Of the latter amount, 96 per cent went to Singapore-headquartered companies, highlighting the concentration of investment within the region. The figures point to the need for a broader funding ecosystem that enables businesses across different markets to develop, validate and scale solutions.
Capital alone, however, will not close the gap. Investment needs to support the full journey from identifying unmet clinical needs and conducting research to validating products, securing regulatory approvals and integrating solutions into healthcare systems. Stronger collaboration between researchers, hospitals, industry and investors can help ensure that products are developed around clearly defined clinical requirements rather than technology availability alone.
The WEF's innovation analysis also highlights the need to direct funding towards conditions with a high disease burden, strengthen the evidence base focused on women's health and expand product development beyond established areas. For Asia-Pacific, this means generating more region-specific evidence, improving the availability and governance of health data, and supporting clinical research that reflects the region's diverse populations.
UN ESCAP recommends increasing funding for women's health research, raising awareness, addressing social taboos and supporting sector-specific incubators, accelerators and networks. Grants and other forms of financial support will be important in helping femtech businesses develop and scale their solutions. Healthcare systems must also ensure that promising innovations can be adopted beyond well-resourced urban centres.
“Looking ahead, the next phase of progress in women's health will depend not only on scientific breakthroughs but also on ensuring broader access to those innovations. Expanding screening programmes, strengthening healthcare systems, generating more APAC-specific evidence, and investing in education and clinical capabilities will be essential to improving outcomes for women and families across the region,” said Kyon.
The economic case for action is substantial. The WEF and MHI report Closing the Women's Health Gap: A $1 Trillion Opportunity to Improve Lives and Economies found that women spend 25 per cent more of their lives in poor health than men. Closing the broader women's health gap could deliver 75 million additional disability-adjusted life years annually and unlock $1 trillion in global GDP each year by 2040.

For Asia-Pacific, the opportunity is not simply to develop more products or adopt new technologies. It is to build a healthcare ecosystem in which women's health needs shape research priorities, clinical evidence guides decisions and innovation reaches the patients it is intended to serve. The next frontier will be defined by how effectively the region turns scientific progress into equitable, measurable and lasting improvements in women's lives.

Beyond Surveillance: Asia-Pacific’s Next Battle Against AMR November 1, 2026 | Sunday | Analysis | By Ayesha Siddiqui As the world observes World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW) from November 18 to 24, 2026, the focus is increasingly shifting towards translating scientific advances and policy commitments into effective interventions. Across Asia-Pacific, progress in genomic surveillance, laboratory capacity and alternative therapeutic approaches is creating new opportunities to combat drug-resistant infections. However, funding constraints, implementation gaps and limited evidence of improved clinical outcomes continue to challenge the region. What will it take to bridge the gap between scientific progress and patient impact? Image credit- shutterstock Asia-Pacific carries a disproportionate burden of drug-resistant infections. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) 2025 global surveillance report highlighted the scale of the problem, estimating that approximately one in three reported bacterial infections in the WHO South-East Asia Region were resistant to antibiotics. In 2019, an estimated 2.6 million deaths across Asia-Pacific were associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR), of which more than 680,000 were directly attributable to it. In the WHO Western Pacific Region, AMR is projected to cause more than five million deaths and cost up to $148 billion between 2020 and 2030. Strengthening the Regional Response Asia-Pacific remains at the centre of the global AMR challenge, both because of its substantial burden of drug-resistant infections and its growing role in developing solutions. The 2024 United Nations General Assembly High-Level Meeting on AMR marked an important milestone in the global response. Its Political Declaration established a target of reducing global deaths associated with bacterial AMR by 10 per cent by 2030, compared with 2019 levels. In May 2026, the World Health Assembly adopted an updated Global Action Plan on AMR for 2026–2036. At the regional level, the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia facilitated the endorsement of a roadmap to accelerate action against AMR in the human health sector for 2025–2030. Member States have also adopted a regional resolution to strengthen their commitment to tackling AMR. Across the wider region, countries continued to update their national action plans, with 19 implementing their second national plans and two their third in 2025. India and Singapore have also strengthened their national responses. India launched its second National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR 2.0) in November 2025, focusing on awareness, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, and intersectoral coordination. Singapore launched its second National Strategic Action Plan on AMR (NSAPv2) in November 2025, building on its One Health approach across human health, animals, food and the environment. “In recent times, some of the most significant developments have included the WHO South-East Asia Region's 2025–2030 AMR roadmap, continued investments in surveillance and laboratory capacity, and increasing efforts to turn national action plans into practical, funded interventions. These are important steps, but they also highlight a broader reality: progress against AMR depends on connecting surveillance, research, innovation, and access,” said Dr Richard Alm, Chief of Research and Development at CARB-X, (Combating Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria Biopharmaceutical Accelerator), a global non-profit partnership that accelerates early-stage research and development of new antibiotics, vaccines and rapid diagnostics to combat drug-resistant bacteria. “Addressing AMR requires change across the healthcare ecosystem” November 1, 2026 | Sunday | Opinion | By Ankit Kankar As antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to threaten patient safety and healthcare outcomes across Asia, the need for responsible antibiotic use has become increasingly urgent. Ahead of World AMR Awareness Week 2026, BioSpectrum Asia speaks with Adjunct Associate Professor Keith Lim Hsiu Chin, Group Chief Medical Officer, IHH Healthcare, about the growing AMR challenge, the importance of antimicrobial stewardship, and how hospitals, healthcare professionals and patients can work together to preserve antibiotic effectiveness and strengthen patient care. For patients and caregivers, what does antimicrobial resistance (AMR) actually mean in practical terms, and how could it affect the treatment of what might otherwise be considered a routine infection? Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites develop resistance and no longer respond as effectively to the antimicrobials designed to treat them. In the case of antibiotics, resistance occurs when bacteria change over time and no longer respond as effectively to the antibiotics used to treat them. This can turn a straightforward infection into one that is more difficult to treat, requiring the patient to take additional tests, a different medication, a longer course of treatment or spend more time in hospital. In more serious cases, fewer treatment options may be available. This is already a significant concern. The World Health Organisation (WHO) Global Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance Report 2025 found particularly high levels of antibiotic resistance in Southeast Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean regions, where almost one in three common bacterial infections was resistant to antibiotics. WHO also notes that AMR undermines life-saving treatments and increases the risks associated with common infections and routine medical interventions. Surgery, cancer treatment, intensive care and the management of patients with weakened immune systems can become riskier if infections cannot be treated reliably. For patients and caregivers, antibiotics should be used only when they are genuinely needed and exactly as prescribed. Protecting their effectiveness is important as it affects patient safety and quality of care. Patients often expect antibiotics when they have an infection. How do clinicians determine when antibiotics are genuinely necessary, and how can healthcare professionals better communicate the decision not to prescribe them? One common misconception is that antibiotics can treat all infections. But in fact, they only work against bacteria and not viruses. The starting point should always be the clinical needs of the patient. Clinicians consider the patient's symptoms, examination findings, medical history, underlying risk factors and the severity of the illness. Diagnostic and laboratory tests can determine whether a bacterial infection is present and which treatment is likely to work. Communication is just as important. Clinicians should explain what is likely causing the illness and why an antibiotic would not help in that particular case. They should also discuss how symptoms can be managed, how long recovery may take and which warning signs should prompt further medical attention. This helps patients understand the recommended treatment and reinforces confidence in the care they receive. What does responsible antibiotic use and antimicrobial stewardship look like within a hospital setting, particularly when clinicians must balance the immediate needs of an individual patient with the longer-term challenge of AMR? Good antimicrobial stewardship is about using the right antibiotic for the right patient, at the right time and for the right duration. This means providing effective treatment today while minimising unnecessary antibiotic exposure that can contribute to resistance over time. IHH Healthcare is the first multinational healthcare provider to implement the CDC's Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme (ASP) Core Elements across its entire network of hospitals. One practical example is the antibiotic “time-out”. In an acutely unwell patient, clinicians may have to begin treatment before all diagnostic or laboratory results are available. Within 48 to 72 hours, they can review the patient’s response, available results and decide whether the treatment should be continued, narrowed, adjusted or stopped. This forms part of a Group-wide Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme aligned with CDC, WHO and relevant national guidelines. The programme includes country-level stewardship committees and treatment guidelines for common infections and procedures. It also incorporates antimicrobial-use audits, post-prescription feedback, antibiograms, infection monitoring, therapy optimisation, pre-authorisation requirements for certain antimicrobials, infection-based interventions and continuing education. Going forward, IHH will continue to measure and track our hospitals’ compliance with ASP protocols, supporting ongoing improvement across our network. How significant is inappropriate or unnecessary antibiotic use in driving AMR across Asia, and what behavioural changes among patients, caregivers and healthcare professionals could make the greatest difference? Inappropriate and unnecessary antimicrobial use is an important driver of AMR, particularly in a region where antibiotic resistance is already substantial. This is influenced by patient expectations, prescribing practices, access to medicines, the availability of diagnostics, healthcare infrastructure, regulation, surveillance and public understanding. Addressing AMR therefore requires change across the healthcare ecosystem. For patients and caregivers, one important shift is understanding that antibiotics are not appropriate for every infection. Patients should avoid self-medicating, sharing them with others, or using leftover medicines from an earlier illness. When antibiotics are prescribed, they should be taken exactly as directed. For healthcare professionals, the responsibility is to continually assess whether an antimicrobial is clinically indicated. Treatment should be informed by the best available evidence and local resistance patterns. It should then be reviewed when more diagnostic information becomes available. Education is therefore important for patients, caregivers and healthcare professionals. At IHH, continuing education forms part of the Group’s ASP, alongside treatment guidelines, monitoring and clinical reviews. Looking towards 2027 and beyond, what changes would you like to see across hospitals and the wider healthcare ecosystem to strengthen antimicrobial stewardship, and how can measurable targets help translate AMR commitments into tangible outcomes? There is already broad recognition that AMR is a serious healthcare threat. The next step is moving from awareness and commitment to measurable improvement. Antimicrobial stewardship should increasingly be embedded within clinical quality and patient safety, rather than as a standalone programme or annual awareness initiative. Healthcare organisations need to be able to answer specific questions: Are antibiotics being prescribed appropriately? Are prescriptions being reviewed when new diagnostic information becomes available? Are broad-spectrum antibiotics being narrowed where possible? Are avoidable infections being prevented? What are local resistance patterns showing? And when one hospital identifies an intervention that works, can that learning be applied more broadly? This is where measurable targets become important. A similar principle is being applied to antimicrobial stewardship. In May 2026, IHH entered a S$250 million sustainability-linked loan with DBS, with financial terms linked to improving responsible antibiotic practices across IHH’s hospitals in Singapore. This is a significant milestone because it connects financing with a defined clinical stewardship indicator, creating greater accountability for translating an AMR commitment into measurable practice improvement. AMR requires sustained collaboration among healthcare providers, governments, regulators and communities. Ultimately, antimicrobial stewardship should be embedded in everyday clinical practice and measured as part of clinical quality and patient safety. It should not be viewed as a separate activity, but as an integral part of safe, effective and responsible care. Asia Pacific Unites to Rewrite the Breast Cancer Equation November 1, 2026 | Sunday | Opinion | By Ahmed Elhusseiny, Area Head, Asia Pacific, Roche Pharmaceuticals Asia Pacific is intensifying efforts to address breast cancer through ASEAN’s regional prioritisation, advances in targeted therapies and collaborative healthcare models that promote earlier detection, faster diagnosis and timely treatment. With HER2-positive breast cancer imposing significant health and economic costs, stronger public–private partnerships, patient-centred care and investment in early intervention could improve survival, reduce healthcare burdens and help the region contribute to the WHO goal of saving 2.5 million lives from breast cancer by 2040. Asia Pacific is helping set the next milestone in global action on breast cancer. ASEAN’s latest decision to elevate breast cancer prevention and control as a regional health priority is one encouraging example of this momentum, marking the first time a cancer-related issue has been designated as a regional focus. The region carries a disproportionate share of the global breast cancer burden, accounting for approximately 48 per cent of new breast cancer cases globally and 45 per cent of breast cancer deaths. At the same time, scientific progress is rapidly expanding the tools available to respond. Take HER2-positive breast cancer, an aggressive sub-type that accounts for approximately 23 per cent of breast cancer cases in Asia. Until recently, it often had a poor prognosis. Advances in understanding how the HER2 protein drives tumour growth have enabled more targeted approaches and have helped improve outcomes in both early and advanced disease. As science continues moving forward, this regional commitment to collective action creates a real opportunity to translate what’s now possible into meaningful change for women, health systems and society. Acting earlier for greater progress What taking on this opportunity looks like may differ in each setting, as different economies have different starting points, resources and models of care. But progress is strongest when health systems help women with breast cancer to move quickly and smoothly from awareness and screening to diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. For women, finding and treating breast cancer earlier can mean a stronger chance of survival; for society, it means greater opportunities to realise the full value of innovation. Evidence shows early-stage treatment is 2.5–3 times more cost-effective than treating metastatic disease and WHO analysis shows that every $1 invested in early diagnosis and comprehensive breast cancer care could generate up to $7.8 in returns. When a woman is diagnosed and treated earlier, she is more likely to live longer in better health, with more time to pursue her goals, build a career, care for others and contribute to her community. Earlier intervention can also reduce pressure on health systems by preventing avoidable complications, reducing the need for more intensive care and easing pressure on health workforce capacity. New research from the independent economic research institute WifOR, commissioned by Roche, brings the scale of the opportunity into focus for Asia Pacific. Covering 11 Asia Pacific economies with diverse health systems and economic contexts, the study estimates that between 2017 and 2027, HER2-positive breast cancer alone will result in approximately 4 million years of healthy life lost and an estimated $116 billion in productivity losses. The study also assessed Roche HER2-positive breast cancer medicines. It estimates they are associated with around 21,300 quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and $1.65 billion in social impact over the same period, with 63 per cent of that impact coming from women treated early. QALYs reflect both living longer and living with better quality of life. Together, these findings strengthen the case for treating breast cancer earlier as a health and socioeconomic opportunity which the region is increasingly moving towards. Adapting care delivery with collective action and shared accountability Ensuring every woman with breast cancer can get high-quality care when and where they need it is not an easy task, particularly in a highly diverse region like Asia Pacific, where care pathways, capacity and geography vary widely. Today, up to 25 per cent of patients in Asia are still diagnosed when their breast cancer has already spread to other parts of the body. Adapting the way care is delivered for earlier detection, faster diagnosis, and quicker connection to appropriate treatment requires whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches. This is where more coordinated action and stronger implementation across the region can help accelerate progress for women, and for the health systems that serve them. The region already has successful collaborations underway. Indonesia is developing a unified National Breast Cancer Action Plan aligned with the WHO Global Breast Cancer Initiative, supported by city-level pilots in Jakarta and Yogyakarta. These pilots bring together ecosystem mapping, shared governance, patient navigation, and public–private–community partnership, with lessons intended to inform broader national implementation. In Malaysia, similar collaborations are enabling more flexible models of care and mobilising wider health-system capacity to bring cancer services closer to women in their communities. For example, the country is scaling from a single national hub to eight regional centres, complemented by district-level clinics that extend access into local communities. In Sabah, a Nursing Privileging Programme has enabled certified local nurses to administer systemic therapies nearer to patients. This approach has since been incorporated into the national nursing curriculum in partnership with the government. Roche works alongside health systems and partners on these efforts, contributing scientific expertise and practical experience, so that advances in science translate into real-world impact for women. With ASEAN establishing a regular regional breast cancer policy dialogue, there will be more opportunities to share effective models of collaboration like these across health systems. Lessons from implementation on the ground can help countries adapt and scale proven approaches, while informing the design of more connected and responsive care systems. What comes next The WHO Global Breast Cancer Initiative set the goal of saving 2.5 million lives by 2040. Asia Pacific has a critical role to play in reaching this target. Decisions and actions on how we value, prioritise and deliver breast cancer care earlier and at scale will have a deep and lasting impact on women, health systems and societies. With advances in science, stronger partnerships and growing leadership, the region is well positioned to translate ASEAN’s priority into practical implementation. The value of this work will be counted first in women’s health, and then in what healthier women can contribute to their families, workplaces and communities. Beyond the region, Asia Pacific’s experience can also offer a practical reference point for global progress on breast cancer and for the broader cancer care community. With ASEAN establishing a regular regional breast cancer policy dialogue, there will be more opportunities to share effective models of collaboration like these across health systems. Lessons from implementation on the ground can help countries adapt and scale proven approaches, while informing the design of more connected and responsive care systems.
What comes next
The WHO Global Breast Cancer Initiative set the goal of saving 2.5 million lives by 2040. Asia Pacific has a critical role to play in reaching this target. Decisions and actions on how we value, prioritise and deliver breast cancer care earlier and at scale will have a deep and lasting impact on women, health systems and societies. With advances in science, stronger partnerships and growing leadership, the region is well positioned to translate ASEAN’s priority into practical implementation.
The value of this work will be counted first in women’s health, and then in what healthier women can contribute to their families, workplaces and communities. Beyond the region, Asia Pacific’s experience can also offer a practical reference point for global progress on breast cancer and for the broader cancer care community.

Japan's Otsuka BioVentures begins strategic equity investments October 28, 2026 | Wednesday | News To provide portfolio companies with access to Otsuka Pharmaceutical's expertise in drug development and commercialisation Image credit- shutterstock Japan-based Otsuka Pharmaceutical has announced that Otsuka BioVentures, LLC (OBV), a corporate venture capital (CVC) firm has begun strategic equity investments. OBV will make strategic equity investments in promising startup companies developing innovative science and technologies that complement and expand Otsuka Pharmaceutical's internal R&D efforts in its key focus areas including psychiatry, neurology, nephrology, and immunology. Through these investments, OBV aims to provide portfolio companies with access to Otsuka Pharmaceutical's expertise in drug development and commercialisation, while broadening access to cutting-edge science and technologies and fostering opportunities for future partnerships In June of this year, OBV participated in the Series B financing round of US-based SonoThera Therapeutics as its first investment. SonoThera is developing a non-viral gene therapy platform that utilises ultrasound technology for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The proceeds from the financing are expected to support the advancement of these programs. OBV has already made its second investment and continues to actively pursue investment opportunities in promising life sciences companies.
